1. Core Clinical Tension: A 23-year-old Nigerian man presenting with 12 months of progressive colicky left loin pain. Radiography and intravenous urography demonstrate left hydroureteronephrosis with two distal ureteric stenoses and calcification at the site of obstruction, prompting an initial working diagnosis of obstructive urolithiasis (ureteric calculus). Although the patient had a remote episode of painless terminal hematuria 2 years earlier treated with antiparasitic medication and subsequent avoidance of freshwater streams, urine microscopy was negative for hematuria or ova/parasites, obscuring chronic granulomatous scarring and calcification caused by bilharzial infection.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission clinical triage captures the history of freshwater stream contact in rural Nigeria, past treated painless terminal hematuria, 12 months of colicky flank pain, unremarkable physical examination, normal renal biochemistry (electrolytes, urea, creatinine), negative urine microscopy/cultures (4-5 WBC/HPF, no RBCs, no ova/parasites), ultrasound revealing left pelvicalyceal dilatation, and intravenous urography showing left hydroureteronephrosis with distal stenoses and focal calcification. The breakpoint is set immediately before operative exploration (ureteroneocystostomy) and histopathological evaluation.
3. Differential Distinctions: Obstructive ureteric calculus is the most likely initial presumptive diagnosis due to colicky flank pain and localized calcification on plain urography, but surgery revealed strictured fibrotic tissue without any intraluminal stone. Bacterial pyelonephritis / UTI is ruled out by sterile urine cultures and absence of constitutional symptoms. Primary ureteral urothelial neoplasm or retroperitoneal fibrosis are rare in this demographic, but the endemic geographic history of stream swimming and distal ureteral bilharzial calcification point toward chronic late parasitic sequelae.
case_prompt:
A 23-year-old Nigerian undergraduate male presents with a 12-month history of insidious, progressive, colicky left loin pain. He reports no lower urinary tract symptoms, gross hematuria, loin swelling, weight loss, or cough, and has no history of retroperitoneal surgery. He grew up in a rural community in southwestern Nigeria where he frequently swam in a local shallow freshwater stream that served as the community's primary water source. Two years prior to presentation, he experienced an episode of painless terminal hematuria that was treated with oral antiparasitic medication resulting in complete resolution of bleeding; following medical counseling, he has avoided freshwater streams and relocated to an urban setting.

On physical examination, he appears well. Abdominal and flank examinations are unremarkable, with no palpable loin mass or tenderness.

Serum electrolytes, urea, and creatinine are all within normal limits. Urine microscopy reveals 4 to 5 white blood cells per high-power field, with no red blood cells and no ova or parasites seen. Urine bacterial culture shows no growth.

Renal ultrasonography reveals dilatation of the renal calyces and pelvis on the left side, with a grossly normal right kidney and ureter. Intravenous urography demonstrates marked dilatation of the left renal calyces, pelvis, and ureter, associated with two discrete areas of stenosis at the distal portion of the left ureter. The plain radiograph demonstrates calcification at the site of obstruction, leading to an initial clinical impression of obstructive ureteric lithiasis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as the initial working diagnosis because of colicky flank pain, left hydroureteronephrosis, and radiographic calcification at the distal ureteric obstruction; however, intraoperative surgical exploration confirmed strictures but found no intraluminal calculus.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Initial diagnosis of ureteric obstruction secondary to calculi was made. Intra-operatively, the findings on urography were confirmed, no calculus was seen and the bladder was grossly normal (Figure 2).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given low-grade pyuria (4-5 WBC/HPF) and flank pain, but excluded by sterile urine cultures, absence of dysuria, and lack of systemic inflammatory signs.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: There were no ova or parasite seen in the urine and no bacterial growth on incubation. Serum electrolyte, urea and creatinine were all within normal limits.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Histopathological analysis of the resected strictured ureteric segment revealed a fibromuscular mass packed with numerous Schistosoma eggs within the ureteric wall, reflecting delayed chronic granulomatous stricturing and calcification despite prior treatment.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Histopathology report however showed a left ureteric mass with numerous Schistosoma ova within the ureteric wall (Figure 3).

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case for urinary schistosomiasis presenting as delayed chronic ureteric stricture and calcification mimicking urolithiasis. Admission breakpoint set prior to surgical excision.
